A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
molecular crowding has an important effect on long range protein ET, which can be rationalized by the dynamical coupling between the redox site, the surrounding protein milieu and the solvent.
the protein scaffold plays a key role in determining the frictional control on ET, and that this control is stronger in the case of a mononuclear copper center.
crowding agents, such as polyvinyl alcohol (PVA), are able to modulate protein electron transfer rates by altering the protein's dynamical coupling to the surrounding medium.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the ET rate is not simply a function of the electronic coupling, but is also dictated by the frictional coupling between the protein redox site and its milieu.
the effect of crowding on protein ET is not a mere viscosity effect but is strongly dependent on the specific properties of the redox active site and of the protein scaffold.
the effect of molecular viscosity on ET rates is determined by the dynamical coupling between the metal site and its environment, which in turn depends on the overall protein scaffold.
